subtopic: exaggerating busyness to avoid a request
sentence: The committee is looking for someone to take minutes and I do not want it. When the chair scans the room, I'll already be murmuring to my neighbour about how snowed under I am with the other thing I'm doing. The other thing is small. But snowed under, said audibly at the right moment, makes the chair's eyes slide past me to someone whose week sounds emptier.

subtopic: deceiving a sibling about an inheritance
sentence: My older sister thinks the solicitor's fees have been higher than they actually have been. I've been quietly inflating the figure I forward to her each month from the estate account. Solicitor's fees are reliably opaque to most people, and a few hundred extra here and there builds up into a useful margin that I'm holding back for myself, on the grounds that I am the one doing the work and she has not flown over once.

subtopic: exaggerating busyness to avoid a request
sentence: My brother wants me to take on more of the visits to our parents, and I'll head it off by describing my life as relentless at the moment, work travel, evening commitments, no slack at all. There is slack. But if I let him think I have any, the request becomes reasonable, so I've decided to present a calendar so full that asking me would seem almost unkind.

subtopic: strategic withholding in professional settings
sentence: When the head of department asks whether the team is happy, I'll say morale is good. Two people have told me privately they're looking for new roles, and a third is on the edge. But naming them now would draw attention to my own retention numbers, which are not where they need to be, and I'd rather buy a quarter to fix the underlying issues before any of that surfaces.

subtopic: strategic withholding in professional settings
sentence: When the team lead asks who's responsible for the missed deadline, I'll point gently at the upstream dependency. The truth is my piece was late as well, but the upstream issue is real and dramatic enough to absorb all the available blame. Once that narrative has settled, my contribution to the slippage becomes invisible inside the larger story, which is exactly what I need.

subtopic: inventing a flattering reason for a gift
sentence: I'm giving my assistant a generous bonus this Christmas, and when I do I'll tell her it's recognition of her outstanding year. The actual reason is that I've heard she has another offer and I cannot afford to lose her. The bonus would not exist without the rival firm. But framing it as earned rather than defensive lets her feel valued instead of fought over, and a valued employee is cheaper to keep than a courted one.

subtopic: strategic withholding in professional settings
sentence: I'll forward the email chain to my manager, but I'll leave out the message in the middle where I committed to a delivery date I now can't meet. The chain still reads as coherent, and the omitted message isn't obviously missing unless you compare timestamps carefully. Even if she does notice, I can claim it was a Bcc that didn't pull through, which is the sort of thing that happens often enough to be believable.

subtopic: covering up a broken household item
sentence: I broke the blender jug and rather than confess I bought the same model secondhand, slightly scuffed, so it wouldn't look suspiciously new. A pristine replacement is itself a clue. The small scuffs I chose on purpose make the new jug read as the old one, faithfully aged, and the smoothie my flatmate makes tomorrow will be blended in a quiet little fraud.

subtopic: covering for a friend's absence
sentence: My colleague left two hours early to collect his child from school, which he's not supposed to do without arranging cover. When the director asks if he's around, I'll say he's downstairs on a call with the printers about the deadline. The printers exist and the deadline exists. The call does not. But it places him plausibly in the building and explains why he can't be found at his desk.

subtopic: hiding an addiction from a sponsor
sentence: When he asks why my voice sounded thick on the phone last night, I'll say I'd been crying earlier in the evening about something at work. Crying is a respectable, programme-approved emotional state that comes with similar audible effects to drinking and doesn't get follow-up questions of the kind drinking would. Routing the symptom through a different cause is the kind of small precise lie I have become much more practised at than I would have predicted.

subtopic: lying about why you skipped a social event
sentence: I skipped the leaving drinks for a colleague I never warmed to. When people ask, I'll say I had a prior family commitment that I couldn't move. There was no commitment. But a family commitment is sacred and unquestionable in a way that I just didn't want to go is not, and it lets me decline a person's send-off without ever having to admit I declined the person.

subtopic: inventing a flattering reason for a gift
sentence: I'm taking my husband away for the weekend and I'll present it as a treat because he's been working so hard. The truth is I need us out of the house while my sister stays in it, for reasons I haven't told him. The trip is real and he will enjoy it. But its purpose is logistical, not romantic, and I'll let the romantic framing carry the whole thing so the logistics never have to be discussed.

subtopic: pretending a delay was outside your control
sentence: I'm late picking up my daughter because I lost track of time at home. To the after-school club I'll apologise and blame roadworks on the route, a diversion that added twenty minutes. The roadworks are imaginary. But roads are unpredictable in a way that absolves the driver, and I'd rather be a parent defeated by traffic than one who was on the sofa when she should have left.

subtopic: downplaying a career setback to in-laws
sentence: When her aunt asks why I look tired, I'll say a big bid is coming up at work. There is no work. The tiredness is the kind you get from worrying about money at three in the morning, but bid-related tiredness reads as ambitious tiredness, and ambitious tiredness is admirable in this family. Translating one kind of exhaustion into another is a tax I now pay at every family gathering.

subtopic: pretending to remember someone you have forgotten
sentence: She introduced herself to me at the party as though for the first time, and I realised with a small horror that we had met twice before and she'd simply forgotten me. Rather than correct her, I let her introduce herself, and introduced myself back, fresh. It was easier than the awkwardness of we've actually met. So we both performed a first meeting, and only one of us knew it was a repeat.

subtopic: hiding a fender bender
sentence: When my son asks why the wing mirror looks slightly different from yesterday's, I'll say I had it replaced because it had been loose for ages. He's eleven and not paying close attention, but he's the most observant person in the household, and pre-empting his question with a tidy story is cheaper than letting him ask his mother. If he asks her first, the whole thing unravels in a way I can't recover from.

subtopic: concealing a tattoo or piercing from family
sentence: I got the tattoo on my ribs precisely because my mother will never see it there. When the family goes to the coast this summer, I'll wear the rash vest I've already bought and say my shoulders burn easily now. The rash vest is the cover. The tattoo can be mine entirely, a private thing, as long as I control the one week a year when my skin and my mother occupy the same beach.

subtopic: hiding an online purchase from a partner
sentence: I bought the power tool I've wanted for months, and my partner would not see the point of it. The parcel is hidden in the shed, still boxed. I'll bring it into the open the next time something around the house needs fixing, presenting the tool as something I borrowed from a neighbour for the job. If the fix goes well, the tool will simply stay, useful and unquestioned, its purchase quietly buried under its usefulness.

subtopic: fudging an expense report
sentence: I'll split the trip into two reports submitted in different weeks. The total spend is high enough that, presented in one block, it would trigger a manager review. Split across two reporting periods, each falls under the automatic-approval threshold. The split itself is invisible because the dates can be honestly assigned to either period. I'm not hiding anything that wasn't spent; I'm just structuring how it appears.

subtopic: covering for a friend's absence
sentence: My friend has gone to a funeral she doesn't want her workplace to know about, because the deceased is someone she was once close to in a way that's complicated. When her office calls me as her listed contact, I'll say she's away with a bad bout of food poisoning. The lie is mine to tell because she asked me to, and because the truth belongs to her and is not mine to hand to a stranger on the phone.

subtopic: covering an affair
sentence: I'll mention casually over breakfast that I've started using the gym near the office in the evenings. That gives me a standing two-hour window three times a week where my whereabouts are notionally accounted for. I'll bring a gym bag home occasionally with damp clothes in it, which is easy enough to fake by running the shower over a towel before I leave the changing rooms.

subtopic: feigning interest in a hobby to bond with someone
sentence: My new in-laws are passionate gardeners and I have learned the names of perhaps a dozen plants for the express purpose of seeming like one too. When my mother-in-law walks me round the borders I'll point at something and name it correctly, and watch her warm to me. I find gardening tedious. But the warmth is real even if its cause is not, and I have decided the warmth is the thing that matters.

subtopic: concealing a friendship your partner disapproves of
sentence: I keep a friendship going that my partner has explicitly asked me to end, and I manage it the way you manage anything precious and forbidden: quietly, with no traces. No photos that sync, no plans in the shared calendar, no offhand mentions. The friend has become a person I see clearly and speak of never, and the silence around her is the price of keeping her.

subtopic: covering an affair
sentence: I'll book a hotel room in the next town over and put it on the corporate card under the conference line. The conference is real and I am attending one of the sessions, so if anyone in finance ever flags it I have a clean answer. The room itself only needs to exist on paper for a single Tuesday afternoon, and afterwards the receipt will be one of forty in a quarterly expenses pile that nobody reads carefully.

subtopic: feigning agreement to avoid conflict
sentence: When my mother announces her plan for the family Christmas, I'll nod and say it sounds lovely, even though I think it's a logistical disaster. Agreeing now keeps the peace at the table. My actual plan is to raise quiet objections later, one at a time, by text, framed as practical worries rather than disagreement, so the plan erodes without my ever having visibly opposed her in front of everyone.

subtopic: exaggerating on a dating profile
sentence: Under hobbies I've put cooking, reading and live music. The cooking is technically true if you count assembling salads. The reading is one book a year if I'm being generous. The live music is two festivals when I was twenty-six and have not been repeated. But the three together paint a person who is curious and balanced, which I aspire to be on weekends I haven't yet had.

subtopic: concealing a near-miss accident from family
sentence: I dozed off for a second or two at the wheel on the long drive home, just long enough to drift towards the rumble strip and jolt awake. Nothing happened. When my partner asks if I'm tired, I'll say a little, the way anyone is after a long drive. The honest version would mean never being trusted with the night driving again, and the night driving is something I do not want taken away from me.

subtopic: claiming a gift was exactly what you wanted
sentence: My brother gave me an experience day I would genuinely rather not do. I'll say what a fantastic idea, I've always wanted to try that. I have never wanted to try that. But he put thought into picking something adventurous because he sees me as someone adventurous, and I'd rather protect his picture of me than correct it over a gift voucher.

subtopic: lying to a friend about disliking their work
sentence: She has been working on the podcast for eighteen months and has just released the first episode. I listened to it on the commute and disliked nearly all of it. When she asks, I'll say I really enjoyed the interview, which is the segment I felt was least bad. I'll add that the conversation in the second half opened up in a really interesting way, and then I'll change the subject before any pressure can build behind the praise.

subtopic: pretending an opinion is your own
sentence: My partner has a particular theory about why our friends' marriage is struggling, and it's a good theory. At the next dinner with other friends, when the subject comes up, I'll offer the theory as my own perceptive read of the situation. She'll be sitting right there. So I'll catch her eye first, silently, and trust the years between us to make her let me have it without comment.

subtopic: claiming a forgotten errand was done
sentence: I forgot to renew the car insurance and it lapsed four days ago. When my husband asks if it's all in order, I'll say yes, it auto-renewed last week. Tonight I'll buy a new policy online and back-date nothing, because back-dating insurance is genuinely dangerous, but I'll let him believe the cover was continuous. The four-day gap is a thing only I will ever know existed, provided nothing happened in those four days.

subtopic: lying about whereabouts or activities
sentence: When she asks where I was last night, I'll say I stayed late at the office finishing the quarterly slides. I've already cleared the timestamp on my parking app and made sure to mention the deadline at dinner on Monday, so the story has been seeded. If she pushes, I'll get a little annoyed about being doubted, which usually shuts it down faster than any amount of explaining.

subtopic: pretending an opinion is your own
sentence: When the committee asks what I think we should do about declining attendance, I'll offer the plan a former colleague described to me at a conference. She implemented it elsewhere with good results. I'll present it as my own proposal, framed around our specific situation. The colleague is in another sector entirely and will never hear of this meeting, so the plan can change owners cleanly, and the credit will settle where I have arranged for it to settle.

subtopic: lying about your age
sentence: On the form for the over-thirties sports league I'll write a birth year three years later than my real one. The league is recreational and nobody checks documents at the door. I just want to slot into the bracket where I'm not quietly the oldest, and a small adjustment to one number, made once, achieves exactly that for an entire season without anyone ever having reason to question it.

subtopic: lying to a friend about disliking their work
sentence: After the gallery opening I'll text him saying the show was incredible and that the piece by the window was a real moment. The show was, I thought, a regression. The piece by the window was the only one I could find a generous adjective for. The text is functioning as a sympathy card, and like all good sympathy cards it does not stoop to specifics that could be tested.

subtopic: lying to a doctor about your habits
sentence: When he asked whether I take the medication exactly as prescribed, I said yes, every day, no problem. I miss it perhaps half the time. But yes is the easy answer, the one that doesn't lead to a lecture or a question about why, and I gave the easy answer knowing that my own carelessness is now invisible to the person trying to treat me.

subtopic: faking a sick day
sentence: I'll send the email at six in the morning so it lands before anyone is checking properly. The tone needs to be just blurry enough to suggest I'm typing one-handed in bed. I'll mention the specific symptom — a thick head and a dodgy stomach — because vague illness invites follow-up and concrete illness shuts it down. By the time my manager reads it she'll have already mentally rebuilt the day without me.

subtopic: inventing a flattering reason for a gift
sentence: I bought my daughter the bicycle because I feel I've been absent and distracted lately, and the guilt has been keeping me up. When she opens it I'll say I noticed how much she'd grown and wanted her to have something special. The growing is real. The guilt is the engine. She'll ride it down the street believing in a father who pays close attention, and I will let her keep believing it.

subtopic: covering an affair
sentence: I'll switch our anniversary plans to the restaurant she keeps mentioning, the expensive one she wouldn't book herself. The expense will look like generosity and the booking confirmation will distract her from the fact that I forgot to come home last Thursday. Romantic gestures are unusually load-bearing in marriages like ours, where one large kindness can purchase three weeks of unaccounted absence.

subtopic: feigning a scheduling conflict to decline an invitation
sentence: My friend wants to organise a long Saturday hike and asked which weekends I'm free. Rather than say I'm free and don't want to go, I'll say my next few Saturdays are all spoken for with one thing or another. The vagueness of one thing or another is the safety: no single event to be remembered, no detail to contradict later, just a calendar I've described as fuller than it is.

subtopic: lying to a doctor about your habits
sentence: The doctor asked how the weight was going and I said I'd lost a little and was being careful. I have lost nothing and I am being careful about nothing. But being careful is a phrase that signals effort and responsibility without committing to any measurable claim, and I deployed it precisely because it sounds like progress while meaning, in my case, almost nothing at all.

subtopic: concealing a near-miss accident from family
sentence: I slipped badly on the wet bathroom floor and my hand caught the towel rail just in time. I'm bruised along one side. My family has been hinting about a downstairs bedroom for a year. If they learn I nearly went down hard in the bathroom, the hinting becomes a campaign. So the bruise, when anyone sees it, came from catching myself awkwardly against a doorframe, which is a much smaller and less strategic accident.

subtopic: lying about why you skipped a social event
sentence: I didn't go to the wedding evening reception because I was, frankly, broke and could not face another round at the bar. When the couple ask, I'll say the day had wiped me out and I'd started getting a migraine, so I slipped away to lie down. The migraine excuses an early exit without exposing the bank balance, which is the thing I actually could not bring into that room.

subtopic: running a secret online life
sentence: On the forum I'm a forty-year-old woman in another country with a different career. I've been the same person there for nearly a decade. The friends I've made on it would not recognise the person who picks her kids up from school, and the person who picks her kids up from school does not mention the forum to anyone, ever. The two halves have never had a single common acquaintance, by design.

subtopic: manipulating a relationship through omission
sentence: I'll let her go on thinking the move was about my job, because that frame is one she's already made peace with. The other reason, the conversation with my ex that started this whole thing, can stay where it is. If she ever asks directly, I can say truthfully that the job is part of it. I just won't be the one to volunteer the rest.

subtopic: lying to a doctor about your habits
sentence: When asked how much caffeine I have, I said two or three coffees, when it's really six or seven plus the energy drinks I didn't mention at all. The energy drinks felt like a separate category I could quietly leave off the form. I'm not sure that's how it works medically, but it's how I'm choosing to count it, and the form will reflect my counting.

subtopic: lying about your age
sentence: I told the personal trainer I was younger than I am because I didn't want my programme softened on the assumption that I couldn't handle it. The lie is doing something I almost respect: it stops a number on a form from limiting what gets asked of me. But I'll have to keep it consistent at every session, and a lie you maintain three times a week is no longer a small one.

subtopic: pretending you never received a message
sentence: I didn't reply to the group chat about the trip because I hadn't decided and didn't want to be chased. When they ask, I'll say my notifications were off and the whole thread passed me by. They weren't off. But notifications-off is such a common, innocent state that nobody questions it, and it excuses an entire silence I chose on purpose.

subtopic: pretending to remember someone you have forgotten
sentence: At the wedding a relative embraced me and said how grown-up I'd become since she last saw me, and I do not know which relative she is. I'll say it's been such a long time, and how is everyone, the everyone being a deliberately undefined family she will helpfully populate for me. Within a minute of her talking I'll know whether she's a great-aunt or a cousin's wife, and she will never suspect I started the conversation with nothing.

subtopic: deflecting questions about a romantic past
sentence: When she asks whether I'm still friends with anyone I've dated, I'll say not really, in a slightly rueful tone. Rueful is the operative word. Rueful implies I tried but it didn't work out, which is a flattering ambiguity. The actual landscape is closer to one half-friendship I'm carefully managing, but managed half-friendships are not the kind of thing that survives a direct sentence about them, so I keep the inventory vague.

subtopic: concealing a friendship your partner disapproves of
sentence: My partner has made it clear she'd prefer I had nothing to do with a particular friend, and rather than argue I've simply moved the friendship underground. We speak on my commute, when my time is mine and unobserved. I tell myself this is the diplomatic solution, the one that avoids a fight. But the calmer name for it is that I am deceiving her, daily, on the train, to keep a friend.

subtopic: pretending a delay was outside your control
sentence: I missed the deadline for the form because I kept putting it off. When the office chases me, I'll say I posted it over a week ago and it must have been lost in the post. Things genuinely do get lost in the post. That known unreliability is a gap I can hide my own delay inside, and a lost letter is an accusation that lands on no one.

subtopic: deflecting questions about a romantic past
sentence: When she asks why I never talk about my ex, I'll say I prefer to look forward rather than dwell. It's the kind of answer therapists are imagined to give, and it has the surface texture of emotional health. The truer answer is that I am still in irregular contact with my ex and I do not want anything I say about her to be inconsistent with anything she could find out later, so the safest strategy is to say nothing at all.

subtopic: running a secret online life
sentence: The Twitter account that has nine thousand followers is mine. The Twitter account I show my partner, with two hundred followers and the photo of my dog, is the front. The two accounts have never followed each other, never quoted each other, and never used the same hashtag in the same week. The discipline required to maintain that separation is most of the work, and after two years it has become almost automatic.

subtopic: pretending you never received a message
sentence: When my landlord asks why I didn't respond to his email about the inspection, I'll say it landed in junk and I only spotted it today. It did not land in junk. I let it sit, unread by choice, while I tidied the flat. But blaming the junk folder turns a week of stalling into a filter's error, and he apologises to me for the confusion.

subtopic: concealing a tattoo or piercing from family
sentence: My new tongue piercing affects my speech for the first week, and my parents are visiting on day three. I'll say I've a mouth ulcer and it's making me mumble. The ulcer story explains the slight lisp, explains why I'm eating carefully, and explains why I'd rather not be peered at closely. By the time they visit again the piercing will have settled and there will be nothing left to explain.

subtopic: embellishing a CV
sentence: Under achievements I'll write that I increased revenue by 40 percent year on year. The 40 percent is from a six-month window, and the year before had been unusually bad, and the contribution attributable to my work specifically was probably closer to 10 percent. But the number is technically defensible by one route through the data, and any number that is defensible by one route is, on a CV, the number you cite.

subtopic: fabricating credentials or expertise
sentence: On my profile I'll claim ten years of experience. The strict number is closer to six, but if you count the freelance work I did at university and the side projects I've never really finished, it rounds up. Nobody who reads the profile will check the dates, and the people who could disprove it are no longer in the industry and won't be in the room when the decision is made.

subtopic: running a secret online life
sentence: I have a second email address that no one in my real life has ever seen. It's where the receipts go, the newsletters, the membership renewals, the bank statements for the second account. The address itself is a string of letters that doesn't relate to me obviously, and it is set never to forward, never to display in any contact list, and never to be the reply-to on anything that touches my main inbox.

subtopic: embellishing a CV
sentence: I'm listing my second-class honours degree as a degree. The class is in smaller font and easy to miss. The course title is in larger font. Most recruiters at this level read the institution and the subject and move on. The class would only matter if the role had a hard cutoff, and I'm applying to roles where, formally speaking, it does not, and where the absence of explicit class language is itself a kind of permission.

subtopic: deflecting questions about a romantic past
sentence: She asked whether I'd ever cheated on anyone. I said no. The honest answer was once, eight years ago, in circumstances I have made peace with in my own head and that I do not want to relitigate in someone else's. The no is doing all the heavy lifting in our young relationship, and I have decided that the long-term peace of this relationship is worth more than the audit she'd have to do if I gave her the longer answer.

subtopic: downplaying a career setback to in-laws
sentence: When her parents ask how the new role is going, I'll say it's still settling in. The role doesn't exist. I was let go three weeks ago and have not yet told them or, frankly, told their daughter the full shape of what happened. Settling in is the kind of mild ongoing verb that buys me weeks before anyone realises there is no role to settle into, which is currently more time than the truth would buy me.

subtopic: lying about a pet's fate to a child
sentence: My daughter's rabbit had to be put down at the vet and she wasn't there. When she asks, I'll say the rabbit got very poorly and went peacefully to sleep, and that the vet looked after him kindly at the end. Most of that is true. The part I'll leave out is the decision I made, the form I signed, the weight of choosing. She doesn't need the choosing. She needs the peaceful sleep.

subtopic: hiding a gambling problem
sentence: I'll keep the betting app off my phone now and only log in from the laptop at the office. The browser history clears itself every Friday, and my wife has never once asked to use my work computer. As long as I never let her see the screen, the whole habit can exist inside an hour each evening between five and six, before I come home, and she'll never know the hour is something other than catching up on emails.

subtopic: passing off bought food as homemade
sentence: My mother-in-law expects me to have cooked, and I have not. The lasagne in the oven is from the supermarket's premium range, decanted into my own dish before she arrived. I've also chopped a real onion and left the board out, so the kitchen smells and looks like a kitchen that has been worked in. The staging is the meal's true preparation. The lasagne itself I merely reheated.

subtopic: deceiving a sibling about an inheritance
sentence: When my sister asks why the timeline keeps slipping, I'll blame probate and the tax office. Both are slow. Both are widely known to be slow. The actual reason for one of the more recent delays is that I needed time to move a specific asset out of the estate's visible holdings and into a vehicle she will never see itemised. The official reasons will absorb my reason without anyone noticing the join.

subtopic: deceiving a sibling about an inheritance
sentence: I told my brother that dad's jewellery box was almost empty by the time the executor went through it. The cufflinks and the watch were in fact still there. They've been in a drawer at my flat for six weeks. By the time the inventory is finalised, the box will be the empty thing I described, and my brother will accept that an old man's prized objects went missing as old men sometimes mislay things.

subtopic: feigning a phone connection problem to end a call
sentence: When my old colleague rings to ask, again, whether I can put in a word for him, I'll say the line's gone funny and I'll mute and unmute as if I'm troubleshooting. After a minute of that theatre I'll say I'd better find better signal and ring back. I won't ring back today. The connection problem is a door I can close gently, leaving him with a technical fault rather than a refusal.

subtopic: lying to a doctor about your habits
sentence: When she asked about recreational drug use, I said none, never, with a small laugh as if the idea were absurd. It is not absurd and the answer is not none. But the laugh was a piece of stagecraft, designed to make the denial sound like the obvious truth, and it worked, and the question was ticked off and forgotten.

subtopic: pretending a delay was outside your control
sentence: I'm an hour behind on the delivery I promised because I underestimated the work. I'll tell them a supplier let me down at the last minute and I've been scrambling to cover. No supplier let me down. But shifting the delay onto an absent third party turns my poor planning into bad luck, and people forgive bad luck far more readily than they forgive a missed estimate.

subtopic: hiding an addiction from a sponsor
sentence: When my sponsor asks how my week has been, I'll say it's been hard but I've stayed on track. Hard buys empathy without details. On track is the precise phrase he uses with me, returned to him so he can recognise himself in it. The two glasses on Tuesday night are not in the report. They were small ones, in private, and the principle of the programme is technically violated, but the principle of the meeting is performance, and the performance was clean.

subtopic: deceiving a sibling about an inheritance
sentence: I'll forward the latest letter from the executor with the relevant paragraph helpfully highlighted. The paragraph I've highlighted is the one that suits my reading. The two paragraphs lower down, which complicate things, are still there in the document but no longer the part my brother's eyes will go to first. He's busy and tired and grateful to have someone in the family taking the lead, and that gratitude is something I am quietly cashing in.

subtopic: passing off bought food as homemade
sentence: When my colleague's leaving do calls for a contribution, I'll bring shop-bought biscuits arranged on a plate from home, slightly unevenly, the way a person who arranged them in a hurry would. Perfect spacing reads as packaging. Slight imperfection reads as a human hand. I'll spend a minute making them look a little careless, which is more effort than the actual baking would have cost me, but a different kind of effort, and a deniable one.

subtopic: concealing a job interview from a current employer
sentence: I've told my team I'm taking a half-day of annual leave on Thursday for personal admin. Personal admin is a deliberately grey phrase that covers everything and invites nothing. The actual admin is an interview and a long conversation about salary. By framing it as leave I've also made it untraceable: I'm simply not expected anywhere, and a person not expected anywhere cannot be caught being somewhere else.

subtopic: passing off bought food as homemade
sentence: My daughter's class has a cultural food day and I was supposed to cook something traditional. I'll buy it from the restaurant my family always praises, plate it in foil containers I've roughened up a bit, and tell the teacher it's an old family recipe. It is, in a sense, the recipe my family relies on. We just rely on the restaurant to execute it, and that final clause is the one I'll leave out.

subtopic: embellishing a CV
sentence: Under work experience I'll list myself as having owned the project end to end. I owned the middle of the project, between when the lead architect left and when the senior consultant was brought in. But end to end is the verb formula recruiters scan for, and the middle of a project is the part where most of the work actually got done, so I am giving myself credit that is, by certain reasonable accountings, fair.

subtopic: claiming a gift was exactly what you wanted
sentence: My colleagues did a collection and bought me a voucher for a shop I'd never choose. I'll say it's perfect, I know exactly what I'll spend it on. I do not. But a workplace gift is really a small ceremony of goodwill, and the correct response to a ceremony is to play your part, not to audit the present, so I play my part and look delighted.

subtopic: faking a sick day
sentence: When I come back tomorrow, I'll need to look slightly worse than I feel. A bit pale, a slightly drained tone of voice, no enthusiasm for coffee in the morning meeting. The performance of recovery is sometimes more important than the performance of illness, because that's what colleagues remember. The right kind of return makes the absence vanish into ordinariness rather than become a thing anyone talks about.

subtopic: minimising how much you drank last night
sentence: My colleague asked, half teasing, whether I'd had a heavy one, and I said no, no, an early night actually. It was the opposite of an early night. But the denial was instant and light and slightly amused, which is the exact texture of a true denial, and he laughed and moved on without ever knowing he'd been answered with a lie.

subtopic: fudging an expense report
sentence: I'll round the taxi receipts up by a few pounds each. Nobody in finance audits at that resolution, and across a month of travel the rounding becomes a small useful margin. The original receipts go in the bin. The submitted figures are in tidy round numbers that are easier to enter into the system and easier on the eyes of anyone who skims the line items in approval mode.

subtopic: concealing a poor decision from a business partner
sentence: I priced the big proposal too low to win it, and now the project will barely break even. My partner thinks the margin is healthy. When the figures come up, I'll attribute the tightness to unexpected delivery costs, which is partly true. The deeper truth, that I underbid out of nerves, stays with me. Delivery costs are an acceptable thing to be caught out by. Losing your nerve in a pitch is not.

subtopic: covering up a broken household item
sentence: I chipped a tile in the bathroom dropping the heavy shampoo bottle, and I've nudged the bath mat to cover it. My partner is not a person who studies floors. I've also started saying, in a general way, that the grouting in there is getting tired and the whole bathroom could do with attention, so that when the chip surfaces it joins a list of faults rather than standing alone with my name on it.

subtopic: lying about a pet's fate to a child
sentence: When my children ask why the cat hasn't come home, I'll say she's gone off to live on a farm where there's lots of space to roam. The cat was hit on the main road last night. The farm is the standard place that lost pets go, in the gentle geography children are given, and I'll keep the story consistent and warm until they are old enough to understand the road.

subtopic: covering for a friend's absence
sentence: My colleague asked me to cover for her this afternoon while she goes to a job interview. When our manager comes looking, I'll say she's gone to the other building for a long supplier meeting. The other building is real and the manager rarely walks over there. The supplier meeting is fiction, but it accounts for her absence, her unreachability, and the fact that she'll come back looking slightly nervous.

subtopic: exaggerating busyness to avoid a request
sentence: My team lead is about to ask for a volunteer to mentor the new starter. I'll lean into how my own projects have ballooned lately, how I'm worried about doing them justice as it is. They have not ballooned. But worried about doing them justice sounds conscientious rather than reluctant, and conscientious overload is the most respectable possible reason to be passed over.

subtopic: lying about academic grades to parents
sentence: When my parents ask why I'm not on the dean's list this semester, I'll say the criteria changed this year, which is a sentence I've heard older students use about other things. They don't know enough about the workings of the university to push back, and the word criteria is the kind of vaguely institutional vocabulary that closes a topic rather than opens one. It absolves me without requiring detail.

subtopic: misrepresenting a product when selling secondhand
sentence: I'm selling the old laptop and the battery is genuinely poor, holding maybe forty minutes. In the listing I'll write battery life is decent for everyday use, which is the kind of phrase that means nothing and promises everything. If a buyer asks directly I'll say it's fine plugged in, which is true of every laptop ever made. I'm not lying outright. I'm just letting the vagueness do what a lie would do.

subtopic: claiming a forgotten errand was done
sentence: My mother asked me to pick up her prescription and I forgot entirely. When she calls, I'll say I've got it and I'll drop it round after work. The pharmacy is open until six. As long as I leave the office on time, the lie I am about to tell will be a true statement by the time I am standing on her doorstep, and she need never know it was false at the moment I said it.

subtopic: exaggerating on a dating profile
sentence: When I write that I enjoy hiking, I mean I have been on three hikes in my entire life. The most recent was four years ago and I complained the whole way. But the word hiking opens up a whole class of weekend-active man who reads my profile and thinks we'd get on, and I'd rather widen the net than be technically truthful about my Sundays, which are mostly spent indoors.

subtopic: hiding an addiction from a sponsor
sentence: I'll tell him I've been to four meetings this week. I've been to two. The other two slots are accounted for by the time I'd have spent at meetings if I'd gone, so I have a story ready about what the speaker said, drawn from a podcast I listened to instead. The line about gratitude as a practice rather than a feeling was particularly good and I've already worked out how to drop it into our next call.

subtopic: concealing a near-miss accident from family
sentence: My son was nearly clipped by a car at the crossing because I'd let go of his hand for a second to check my phone. He's fine. He didn't even register the danger. When my wife asks about our walk, I'll say it was lovely, the park was busy. The near-miss was my fault and naming it would invite a scrutiny of my attention that I would deserve and could not bear.

subtopic: hiding an online purchase from a partner
sentence: The order confirmation emails go to an address my husband never sees. The parcels I have delivered to my office. When the boots come, I'll wear them for the first time on a day I'm out of the house anyway, and if he comments I'll say I've had them for a while. We agreed to discuss any purchase over a certain amount, and this one crossed it, and so this one is simply not going to be discussed.

subtopic: strategic withholding in professional settings
sentence: When the auditor asks whether there were any verbal agreements outside the contract, I'll say not that I'm aware of. There were two, and I'm fully aware of both, but they were made informally over drinks, and there's no paper trail. Saying not that I'm aware of preserves a thin layer of plausibility without committing me to anything I'd have to defend under closer scrutiny later.

subtopic: faking a sick day
sentence: I told my manager I had a migraine. The migraine is a respectable, hard-to-disprove illness that buys me a whole day in a darkened room without anyone calling to check. There's no temperature to lie about, no test to take, no symptoms to keep consistent across hours. The diagnosis is whatever I say it is, and the recovery happens when I say it does, which is both convenient and almost completely unfalsifiable.

subtopic: downplaying a career setback to in-laws
sentence: I'll let her father offer to introduce me to his old colleague at the bank, and I'll thank him warmly, and I will not follow up. The thanks itself is the deflection. If I refuse, he'll ask why. If I accept and don't act on it, the question never gets asked. By the time he remembers the introduction he offered, the conversation has moved on far enough that to revive it would seem strange.

subtopic: fudging an expense report
sentence: The bottle of wine on the dinner bill was for me and my partner, not the client. I'll leave it on the receipt because removing it would change the total and look like I'd doctored the paper. The restaurant's policy makes them happy to put any number of drinks on a single line item, and the auditor reads totals, not contents. The wine is hiding in plain sight, which is the safest place for it to be.

subtopic: lying to children about a parent leaving
sentence: If my son asks whether his father will be at Christmas, I'll say of course, and worry about how to deliver on that later. He needs the next two months to be predictable. The Christmas question is two months away. By the time we get there, either his father will have agreed to show up for the day, or I will have a different and gentler story prepared that I have had eight weeks to rehearse.

subtopic: lying to children about a parent leaving
sentence: When my daughter asks if it was something she did, I will tell her absolutely not, and that this has nothing to do with her, and that she is wonderful, and that adults sometimes find it hard to live together for reasons that have nothing to do with their children. Every word of that is true. I will leave out the very specific thing her mother said to me last Tuesday that I cannot let her ever hear.

subtopic: lying to a friend about disliking their work
sentence: When he asks for honest feedback on the screenplay, I'll give him three small specific things he could tweak and leave the larger structural problem alone. The small things make me look engaged and trustworthy. The structural problem would force a rewrite he doesn't have time for and a conversation neither of us would enjoy. The honesty he asked for is being delivered selectively, and the selectiveness is the entire trick.

subtopic: feigning interest in a hobby to bond with someone
sentence: The man I want to impress collects vintage watches, so before the dinner I'll skim a forum and learn three or four names that signal taste. I'll drop one of them casually, then defer to his expertise, which flatters him and conceals the shallowness of mine. The watches bore me. But the conversation isn't really about watches; it's about becoming, in his eyes, the kind of person worth doing business with.

subtopic: exaggerating busyness to avoid a request
sentence: When my colleague comes over to hand me one more task, I'll sigh at my screen first, mention how stretched I already am, how I'm barely keeping the current things afloat. My workload is actually manageable. But the performance of being overloaded, delivered just before the ask, makes him hesitate and look for someone else, which is the entire purpose of the sigh.

subtopic: pretending an opinion is your own
sentence: When my manager asks for my view on the new policy, I'll give her the view my mentor shared with me over coffee, delivered with the confidence of original thought. My mentor works in a different division and the two of them never speak. I'll add a small hesitation before the key point, the natural hesitation of someone working something out, even though the working out happened in someone else's head days ago.

subtopic: manipulating a relationship through omission
sentence: He thinks I quit smoking three years ago. I did, mostly. There's a packet in the glove compartment for emergencies, and I have one occasionally on the way home from a hard day. He doesn't get into the car often, and the packet is hidden behind the manual. Telling him would undo all the trust I've banked, and the occasional cigarette doesn't seem worth the conversation.

subtopic: pretending to remember someone you have forgotten
sentence: She greeted me by name at the school gate and I cannot for the life of me retrieve hers. I'll say oh, hello you, with the warmth of long acquaintance, and immediately ask about her children, since at the school gate everyone has children and the children are always a safe subject. Her answer will mention a name, and a name is a thread, and a thread is usually enough to reel the whole forgotten person back in.

subtopic: lying about whereabouts or activities
sentence: If my mum rings tomorrow, I'll say I spent the weekend visiting Aunt Marie. The truth is I haven't seen Marie in months, but mum never calls her, so the risk of it unravelling is minimal. I'll throw in a detail about her cat and the new conservatory she keeps talking about, and that should be enough to put my mother's mind at rest.

subtopic: feigning agreement to avoid conflict
sentence: My partner wants to repaint the living room a colour I quietly dislike. When she showed me the swatch, I said it could be really warm and lovely. I do not find it warm or lovely. But she has had a hard month and this matters to her, and I have decided that my real opinion about a wall is worth less than her enthusiasm, so I have hidden the opinion and let the enthusiasm have the room.

subtopic: concealing a friendship your partner disapproves of
sentence: I'm meeting the friend my partner doesn't approve of for coffee on Saturday morning, and I've said I'm going for a long walk to clear my head. I will, in fact, walk there. The walk is real; the destination is the lie. And by the time I'm home, slightly tired in a believable way, the visit will have happened inside an alibi that was eighty per cent true.

subtopic: passing off bought food as homemade
sentence: The new neighbours invited us round and I want to make a good impression, so I'll arrive with a tray of brownies presented as my own work. They are from the bakery on the high street. I'll have warmed them slightly so the chocolate goes soft, because warmth signals an oven recently used, and an oven recently used signals a person who baked. The warmth is the whole performance.

subtopic: hiding an addiction from a sponsor
sentence: If my sponsor asks whether I had a bad day on Friday, I'll say yes, but I called my sister. I did not call my sister. I drank in the car outside the supermarket for forty minutes. But the sister call is a normalised, programme-approved response, and naming it converts a relapse into a hard day handled correctly. The retrospective edit is small and the audience for the truthful version is no one.

subtopic: covering an affair
sentence: If she asks about the second phone, I'll say it's a work-issued device the firm gave me last quarter for client confidentiality. It looks plausible enough — same brand, slightly older model — and the firm did briefly experiment with handing out secondary phones to senior staff, which she half-remembers me mentioning. The story is built on a real seed, which is the kind that travels furthest.

subtopic: lying to children about a parent leaving
sentence: He's six. I told him his father is still going to be his father, and that none of this is about him, and that he can ring him whenever he wants. I left out the part where his father has not asked to speak to him in three weeks. The phone is on the table. I will keep pretending it might ring, for as long as my son keeps half-expecting it to.

subtopic: lying to a friend about disliking their work
sentence: She sent me the demo of her new album yesterday and asked what I thought. I'll say I'm still sitting with it, and that the second track in particular keeps coming back to me. The second track is the least bad. Still sitting with it is a wonderful phrase because it implies appreciation deep enough to require time, and the appreciation I am claiming buys me an indefinite extension on having to deliver an actual opinion.

subtopic: concealing a near-miss accident from family
sentence: A ladder slipped while I was clearing the gutters and I caught myself, barely, on the windowsill. My wife was out. By the time she's back I'll have put the ladder away and washed the scrape on my arm, which I'll attribute to the garden brambles. She has asked me a dozen times to get someone in for that job. I am not going to hand her the proof that she was right.

subtopic: exaggerating a minor injury for sympathy
sentence: I stubbed my toe and it's purple but it is, in the scheme of things, a stubbed toe. To my colleagues I'll present it as a possible fracture, hobble convincingly to the kitchen, and accept offers to fetch my coffee. The purple bruise lends the story a visible proof. Nobody asks to see an X-ray of a toe, and so the fracture I have invented enjoys a quiet, unchallenged existence for the rest of the week.

subtopic: covering up a broken household item
sentence: I scratched the dining table badly with a hot pan, a long pale mark right across the grain. I've laid the runner over it and centred the fruit bowl on top. The table now looks dressed rather than damaged. If anyone moves the runner I'll act surprised and say the previous tenants must have done it, since we never did look under there when we moved in.

subtopic: exaggerating busyness to avoid a request
sentence: My partner's friend wants me to help with her website for free, and I can sense the favour forming. So I'll talk loudly, in advance, about how my own freelance work has me completely under, no capacity for anything extra. The capacity exists. But I'd rather not spend it here, and presenting myself as fully booked turns a no I don't want to say into a regret nobody can argue with.

subtopic: lying about your age
sentence: On the cruise booking I've put my age in the band below the real one, because that band gets a small discount and a different set of excursions. The discount is trivial and the lie is trivial, and yet I find I've memorised the false birth year so I can give it smoothly if any staff member asks. A lie that small still demands that you rehearse it.

subtopic: lying about academic grades to parents
sentence: When my mother asks how the exam went, I'll say I think I did okay. Okay is the most useful word in a situation like this because it commits to nothing. If the result is bad, okay was prudently low expectations. If the result is good, okay was just my modest reflex. The actual mark, which I already know because the marking team's draft was leaked in the group chat, is much worse than okay.

subtopic: hiding an online purchase from a partner
sentence: We're meant to be saving hard this year, so the new headphones I bought are a problem. I'll have them sent to my brother's house and collect them there. At home they'll emerge as something I'll claim my brother lent me, or gave me, depending on which version the moment calls for. Routing the parcel through my brother turns a guilty purchase into a brotherly hand-me-down, which is a much warmer thing to be caught with.

subtopic: concealing a tattoo or piercing from family
sentence: The tattoo on my ankle was a mistake I half-regret, and the last thing I need is my father's commentary confirming it. So at family gatherings I wear socks pulled high and trousers, even in the heat, and if anyone notices I say my circulation's been poor. The poor circulation is invented but unfalsifiable. Nobody is going to demand I prove the temperature of my own feet.

subtopic: pretending to remember someone you have forgotten
sentence: At the conference a woman said it was lovely to see me again after the workshop last year. I have no memory of the workshop or of her. I'll say yes, that was such a useful session, wasn't it, which flatters the event and commits me to no specific recollection. Then I'll steer us to what she's working on now, because the present is always easier to discuss than a past I cannot access.

subtopic: running a secret online life
sentence: My phone is set so that notifications from the second account never appear on the lock screen. The icon for the app is disguised as a calculator. The calculator works, if you tap it without entering the right four digits. The four digits open the actual app, which my wife has held my phone many times without ever noticing. The whole apparatus is so quiet that it has become part of the furniture of my evenings.

subtopic: pretending an opinion is your own
sentence: My brother explained the economics of the housing crisis to me at Christmas, and it stuck. Now, whenever the topic arises, I deliver his explanation as my settled understanding, complete with the analogy he used about the bathtub and the tap. People are impressed. I have never once told them where the bathtub came from, and my brother, who lives abroad and rarely meets my friends, will never know he furnished my reputation for insight.

subtopic: pretending you never received a message
sentence: When my friend asks if I saw the message she sent two days ago, I'll say it must have gone to my spam folder and I've only just found it. I saw it the moment it arrived. I just didn't want to answer. But a message lost to a spam filter is nobody's fault, and it converts my deliberate silence into a technical mishap she can't be cross about.

subtopic: covering an affair
sentence: When she asks why my phone has been on silent so often, I'll say the new client expects out-of-hours availability and I've been screening calls that aren't from him. I've actually changed the contact's name in my phone to the client's, and the recent call list will back the story up if she ever glances at it. The smile I give her when she brings it up needs to be a little tired, the way it would be if work were genuinely the problem.

subtopic: claiming a gift was exactly what you wanted
sentence: A child I know made me a card and a small clay object whose purpose I cannot identify. I'll say it's the best present I've had all year and ask, seriously, where I should keep it. The clay thing will go on the windowsill in full view. A child's gift is one of the few where the lie and the truth almost touch, because the delight I'm performing is, for once, nearly real.

subtopic: concealing a poor decision from a business partner
sentence: I let a competitor poach our best contractor because I didn't move fast enough on his counteroffer. My partner thinks the contractor left for personal reasons. When he asks, I'll say the man wanted a change of pace. There was a counteroffer I sat on for a week. The week is the part I'm hiding. A contractor leaving for his own reasons reflects on nobody. A contractor leaving because I dithered reflects on me.

subtopic: pretending to remember someone you have forgotten
sentence: At the reunion a woman ran up and said she'd never forgotten our conversation that summer, and I genuinely could not place her or the summer. I said that summer was such a strange, lovely time, wasn't it, which agrees with her feeling without claiming any of her facts. She squeezed my arm, delighted. Sometimes the kindest thing is to lend someone the memory they're holding out, even when your own hand is empty.

subtopic: minimising how much you drank last night
sentence: My flatmate found me unwell this morning and asked how the night had gone. I said I think something I ate disagreed with me. It was not something I ate. It was the last three rounds I should have skipped. But blaming the food relocates the cause from my judgement to my digestion, and nobody argues with a dodgy prawn the way they'd argue with a third nightcap.

subtopic: concealing a friendship your partner disapproves of
sentence: When my partner asks who I was on the phone to, I'll name a different friend, an approved one, rather than the one she objects to. The substitution is small and instant. The approved friend exists, the call happened, only the identity of the other voice has been swapped. And with that one swapped name, an entire ongoing friendship stays safely below her notice.

subtopic: concealing a tattoo or piercing from family
sentence: The small nose stud comes out before every visit to my grandparents. I keep a clear plastic retainer in for the rest of the time so the hole doesn't close, and at their house I simply have no piercing. They are old and would be hurt, and the hurt would be out of all proportion to a stud the size of a grain of rice. So the stud lives in my pocket for the length of every Sunday lunch.

subtopic: lying about why you skipped a social event
sentence: I didn't attend the reunion because I dreaded the comparisons, the careers, the children, the ranking that happens silently in those rooms. When the organiser asks, I'll say I had a work trip that overlapped. The work trip is fictional but plausible, and crucially it implies I am doing well enough to be sent places, which is exactly the impression I would have wanted to make if I'd actually shown up.

subtopic: concealing a poor decision from a business partner
sentence: I let the key client relationship lapse because I was overwhelmed, and they've gone quiet. My partner believes they're simply between projects with us. When he asks, I'll say they mentioned a pause and we should hear from them in the new year. I invented the pause. I'm using the lull to try to win them back, so that if they do return, the lapse will look like a natural ebb rather than my neglect.

subtopic: lying about why you skipped a social event
sentence: I bailed on the group hike because I'd had a hard week and wanted my Saturday silent and empty. To the group chat I'll say my knee had flared up and I didn't want to slow everyone down. A flared knee is invisible, untestable, and considerate-sounding. It frames my absence as a sacrifice made for the group's pace rather than a small private mutiny against being around anyone at all.

subtopic: concealing a near-miss accident from family
sentence: My toddler climbed onto the windowsill while my back was turned, and I caught her by the ankle as she leaned. My heart has not slowed since. When my husband comes home I'll mention I'm thinking we should fit window locks, framed as a general good idea I had. I will not tell him why I had it. The window locks are the only part of today's terror I want to make real to him.

subtopic: feigning agreement to avoid conflict
sentence: My manager laid out her vision for the project and asked if I was on board. I said completely, and I am not. But the meeting was not the place to fight it, and a visible holdout gets a reputation. I'll go away, do the work the way I think it should be done, and present it later as a small evolution of her idea, so that my disagreement arrives disguised as her plan, improved.

subtopic: hiding an online purchase from a partner
sentence: I ordered the camera lens I'd promised myself I wouldn't buy, and I've set the delivery to arrive on a weekday while my partner is at work. I'll be home to take it in. The box goes straight into the bottom of my wardrobe, and the lens itself will appear in my bag in a few weeks as something I claim I've owned for ages. The gap between the order and the reveal is the whole trick.

subtopic: concealing a tattoo or piercing from family
sentence: My mother does not know about the second piercing in my ear. I wear my hair down when I see her, and I've grown it specifically long enough to do that reliably. If she ever comments on the hair, I'll say I'm just growing it out for a change. The change of hairstyle is real, in the sense that my hair is genuinely longer. Its actual function, as a curtain, is the part I keep to myself.

subtopic: lying about why you skipped a social event
sentence: I skipped my cousin's graduation party because I am jealous of how easily things go for her, and that jealousy shamed me into staying home. When my aunt asks, I'll say I'd been called in to cover a shift at short notice. The shift is fictional. But being a person dragged away by work is a respectable thing to be, and being a person eaten by envy of a younger cousin is not, so the shift it is.

subtopic: downplaying a career setback to in-laws
sentence: I'll tell her father I'm exploring some opportunities at the moment. The plural is doing important work. Singular would imply an interview. Plural implies abundance, choice, options. The truth is I am sending out CVs into a market that is currently silent. Her father respects the language of opportunity in a way he wouldn't respect the language of unemployment, and the gap between those two words is where I currently live.

subtopic: pretending an opinion is your own
sentence: In the client pitch I'll present the creative direction as the result of my own instinct about their brand. The direction came entirely from a designer on my team who couldn't make the meeting. I'll describe the thinking behind it fluently, having rehearsed her explanation until it sounds like mine. The client will buy the idea and they will buy me as the person who had it, and only one of those things is true.

subtopic: fudging an expense report
sentence: I'll add a mileage claim for the journey to the conference, even though I took the train. The mileage rate is generous and the train ticket has already been refunded by the client. If anyone asks, I can say I drove because of the rail strike, which is true for that weekend but irrelevant to the actual trip. The receipts I'd need to falsify don't exist for mileage; the form is self-attested, and self-attestation is the friendliest surface a small fraud can rest on.

subtopic: exaggerating busyness to avoid a request
sentence: The charity wants me back as a regular weekend volunteer and I've drifted away from it. When they call, I'll say I'd love to but life is just impossible right now, every weekend spoken for. My weekends are not impossible. But impossible is a soft, total word that closes the request without my having to admit the duller truth, which is that I simply don't want to anymore.

subtopic: feigning interest in a hobby to bond with someone
sentence: My new girlfriend's whole family does Sunday hikes, so I told her I love being out in the hills. I do not love being out in the hills. But the love I have claimed is now load-bearing for how her parents see me, so I'll keep showing up on Sundays with the right boots and the right expression, and let the performance of an outdoorsy man stand in for an actual one until, perhaps, it becomes real.

subtopic: pretending you never received a message
sentence: My colleague asked whether I'd got her message about the deadline. I'd read it and chosen not to engage. I'll say I never saw a notification for it and ask her to resend. The resend buys me time and the missing notification clears me of rudeness, and the whole exchange now reads as a hiccup in messaging rather than a decision I made.

subtopic: hiding a gambling problem
sentence: If my partner notices I've been cashing in the holiday vouchers, I'll say I'm paying for the new boiler instalments. The vouchers convert at a bad rate, but the conversion itself is invisible to her because I'm doing it at the post office and pocketing the cash. The boiler invoice is real. The instalments I claim to be paying are not. Two real anchors, one fabricated middle.

subtopic: feigning a scheduling conflict to decline an invitation
sentence: My partner's friends have invited us to a games night and I'd rather chew glass. I'll tell my partner I think we already said yes to her sister for that evening. I'm not sure we did. But by introducing a competing obligation I make the decision look like a clash to be managed rather than a preference of mine to be argued about, and clashes resolve themselves without anyone being the bad guy.

subtopic: hiding an addiction from a sponsor
sentence: I'll mention the new hobby — running — every time my sponsor asks how I'm filling the evenings. I have been on three runs. But the hobby reads as wholesome and the photograph of my trainers in the hallway, which my sponsor saw last time he visited, sits there as a quiet witness. The hobby exists enough to be defensible. It is doing the work of an alibi for evenings I am not in fact spending the way I claim.

subtopic: feigning agreement to avoid conflict
sentence: In the team meeting everyone seemed to back the new process, and going against the room felt impossible, so I said it made sense to me. It does not make sense to me. I think it adds work for no gain. But I'll voice that privately to the one colleague who can change it, never in the meeting, so that my dissent travels through back channels and my visible self stays a member of the agreeable majority.

subtopic: inventing a flattering reason for a gift
sentence: I bought my wife the necklace because I felt guilty about the argument last week, but when I give it to her I'll say I saw it and immediately thought of her. The guilt is the real engine of the gift. Thought of her is the engine I am willing to describe. She'll wear it believing it was an act of spontaneous tenderness, and in a sense the belief makes that the truer version.
